method: OPEN AND QUOTED, from the RCH Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline 'Intravenous fluids' (Last updated January 2026), retrieved 2026-09-23. Every pass claim is machine re-checkable. LICENCE: Free to read but NOT openly licensed -- each page carries '(c) 2026 The Royal Children's Hospital'. Quoted with attribution on the same footing as the 14 RCH guidelines and the Immunisation Handbook guidelines already in this compendium.

claims.claim: **Treat IV fluid as a prescribed medication; use the enteral route whenever possible.** This guidance applies from 1 month to 18 years.
claims.source_text: Intravenous (IV) fluid therapy should be treated as a prescribed medication with the indications, contraindications and adverse effects considered. Whenever possible, the enteral route should be used … This guideline only applies to children aged 1 month to 18 years who cannot receive enteral fluids
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Intravenous fluids' (Last updated January 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Intravenous_fluids/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Red flags:** sodium under 135 or over 145 mmol/L, or changing by more than 0.5 mmol/L/hr — notify a senior clinician; short gut or major GI pathology; **resuscitation over 20 mL/kg.**
claims.source_text: Abnormal serum sodium <135 mmol/L or>145 mmol/L or significant change of >0.5 mmol/L/hr on a repeat measure. See hyponatraemia or hypernatraemia and notify senior clinician … Short gut or other significant gastrointestinal pathology Fluid resuscitation >20 mL/kg required
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Intravenous fluids' (Last updated January 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Intravenous_fluids/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Weigh at the start and at least daily** — repeated weights are the best measure of fluid status. Record intake and losses with at least 12-hourly subtotals.
claims.source_text: Repeated weights are the best measure of fluid status. All children on IV fluids should be weighed at the start of treatment and then at least once daily … Document intake/inputs and ongoing losses (including urine output), with at least 12 hourly subtotals
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Intravenous fluids' (Last updated January 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Intravenous_fluids/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Check electrolytes and glucose before starting, and at least every 24 hours** while running more than 50% maintenance; recheck at 4–6 hours in sicker children or with large losses or abnormal electrolytes.
claims.source_text: All children should have serum electrolytes and glucose checked before starting IV fluid treatment, and at least every 24 hours if IV fluids are continued at more than 50% maintenance … For more unwell children and children with large fluid losses or abnormal electrolytes, check the electrolytes and glucose 4-6 hours after starting fluid therapy
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Intravenous fluids' (Last updated January 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Intravenous_fluids/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Shock: 10–20 mL/kg sodium chloride 0.9% as fast as possible, reassess after each bolus, repeat 10–20 mL/kg as needed.** Senior clinician at ≥20 mL/kg; **consider inotropes at ≥40 mL/kg.** Bolus volumes are not counted in later calculations.
claims.source_text: Give a bolus of 10-20 mL/kg of sodium chloride 0.9% as fast as possible, and reassess to determine if additional IV fluid is required Do not include this fluid volume in subsequent calculations Reassess circulation after each bolus Give additional boluses 10-20 mL/kg as required If ≥20 mL/kg in fluid boluses, involve a senior clinician If ≥40 mL/kg in fluid boluses, inotropes should be considered
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Intravenous fluids' (Last updated January 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Intravenous_fluids/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Trauma: packed red cells 10 mL/kg first-line.** Plasma-Lyte 148, Hartmann's or albumin only on senior advice.
claims.source_text: Packed red blood cells 10 mL/kg first-line fluid replacement in trauma Plasma-Lyte 148, Hartmann's solution or albumin may sometimes be used as resuscitation fluid on senior advice
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Intravenous fluids' (Last updated January 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Intravenous_fluids/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Never give a glucose-containing fluid as a shock bolus.**
claims.source_text: Glucose containing fluids should not be given as a fluid bolus for shock.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Intravenous fluids' (Last updated January 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Intravenous_fluids/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Maintenance: sodium chloride 0.9% with glucose 5% (± potassium)** in most situations; include glucose (usually 5%) for most children, especially nil by mouth.
claims.source_text: In most situations, the preferred maintenance fluid type is sodium chloride 0.9% with glucose 5% +/- potassium … Glucose (usually 5%) should be included in maintenance fluids for most children, especially those with no other source of glucose eg nil by mouth
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Intravenous fluids' (Last updated January 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Intravenous_fluids/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Alternatives:** Plasma-Lyte 148 with glucose 5% (5 mmol/L potassium, less chloride) for hyperchloraemia and acidosis. Hartmann's with glucose 5% is rarely used and **is incompatible with some drugs, e.g. ceftriaxone.**
claims.source_text: Plasma-Lyte 148 with glucose 5% contains 5 mmol/L potassium and less chloride than sodium chloride 0.9% with glucose 5%. It may be used in children with hyperchloraemia and acidosis Hartmann's solution with glucose 5% is not often used as a maintenance fluid in children, and requires checking for drug incompatibility eg ceftriaxone
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Intravenous fluids' (Last updated January 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Intravenous_fluids/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Potassium chloride 20 mmol/L**, premixed with sodium chloride 0.9% and glucose 5%, once electrolytes and renal function are known.
claims.source_text: Potassium in maintenance fluids Potassium chloride 20 mmol/L Available in premixed bags with sodium chloride 0.9% and glucose 5% Consider once serum electrolytes and renal function have been assessed Use premixed fluid containing potassium where possible
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Intravenous fluids' (Last updated January 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Intravenous_fluids/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Glucose 15–20%** only on senior advice, ideally centrally; **over 20%** only in intensive care.
claims.source_text: Glucose 15-20% Only prescribed with senior clinician advice Very occasionally used in neonates and in children with metabolic disorders Ideally given via central venous access Glucose >20% Only prescribed in intensive care setting
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Intravenous fluids' (Last updated January 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Intravenous_fluids/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Hypotonic fluids (e.g. sodium chloride 0.45%) are not for routine use** — only with a senior clinician or in intensive care; they may cause hyponatraemia.
claims.source_text: Hypotonic fluids Fluids containing a sodium concentration less than plasma are not recommended for routine use in children Sodium chloride <0.9% eg 0.45% Only prescribed in consultation with senior clinician, or in an intensive care setting Rarely indicated Hypotonic fluids may cause hyponatraemia
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Intravenous fluids' (Last updated January 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Intravenous_fluids/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Full maintenance (well children only):** 3–10 kg: 100 mL/kg/day (4 mL/kg/hr); 10–20 kg: 1000 + 50 × (weight − 10) mL/day [40 + 2 × (weight − 10) mL/hr]; 20–60 kg: 1500 + 20 × (weight − 20) mL/day [60 + 1 × (weight − 20) mL/hr]; over 60 kg: normal maximum 2400 mL/day (100 mL/hr). Consider ideal body weight; adjust for all unwell children.
claims.source_text: Weight (kg) Full maintenance mL/day mL/hour 3-10 100 x weight 4 x weight 10-20 1000 + 50 x (weight - 10) 40 + 2 x (weight - 10) 20-60 1500 + 20 x (weight - 20) 60 + 1 x (weight - 20) >60 2400 mL/day is the normal maximum amount 100 mL/hour … Consider using ideal body weight to calculate maintenance fluid rates. This calculation applies for well children only. Fluid rates need to be adjusted for all unwell children
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Intravenous fluids' (Last updated January 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Intravenous_fluids/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Infants: prescribe IV fluid on water requirement (100 mL/kg/day up to 10 kg)**, not the 150–180 mL/kg/day enteral milk volume.
claims.source_text: Babies need a higher volume of enteral milk (150-180 mL/kg/day) to meet nutritional and growth requirements, but this higher volume should not be used as a basis for IV fluid prescribing IV fluid prescribing for an infant should be based on the water requirement (ie 100 mL/kg/day up to 10 kg) and then adjust as clinically indicated (eg restrict to 2/3 maintenance)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Intravenous fluids' (Last updated January 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Intravenous_fluids/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Use 2/3 maintenance in most unwell children unless dehydrated** — high ADH risks water overload and hyponatraemia.
claims.source_text: The majority of unwell children will retain water and require less than full maintenance fluids eg 2/3 maintenance … 2/3 maintenance rates should be used in the majority of unwell children unless they are dehydrated. Unwell children are likely to secrete high levels of antidiuretic hormone (ADH), so will need less fluid to avoid water overload and hyponatraemia
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Intravenous fluids' (Last updated January 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Intravenous_fluids/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Further restriction may be needed (seek senior advice)** in acute CNS conditions, pulmonary conditions including bronchiolitis and ventilation, post-operatively and after trauma.
claims.source_text: Children with the following conditions are at high risk of excess ADH secretion and may require further fluid restriction, seek senior advice: Acute CNS conditions (meningitis, tumours, head injuries) Pulmonary conditions (pneumonia, bronchiolitis, mechanical ventilation) Post-operatively Trauma
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Intravenous fluids' (Last updated January 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Intravenous_fluids/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.source_text: Weight (kg) Full maintenance (mL/hour) Well child eg fasting for elective surgery 2/3 maintenance (mL/hour) Majority of unwell children unless dehydrated 5 20 13 10 40 27 15 50 33 20 60 40 25 65 43 30 70 47 35 75 50 40 80 53 45 85 57 50 90 60 55 95 63 ≥60 100 67

claims.claim: **Replace at most 5% deficit over 24 hours (on top of maintenance), then reassess.** Over 5% dehydrated — e.g. 10% — replace 5% in the first 24 hours and 5% in the next 24.
claims.source_text: When treating dehydration (ie replacing a fluid deficit) with IV fluids, most children should have a maximum of 5% fluid deficit replaced over 24 hours (in addition to maintenance), and then be reassessed to determine ongoing need for IV fluids … For children with ≤5% dehydration, replace deficit in the first 24 hours For children with >5% dehydration, replace deficit over a longer period eg for 10% dehydration, replace 5% deficit in the first 24 hours, then 5% in the following 24 hours
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Intravenous fluids' (Last updated January 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Intravenous_fluids/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Clinician estimates of % dehydration are unreliable** — use a constant rate on premorbid weight and adjust only the duration.
claims.source_text: clinician estimates of % dehydration have been shown to be unreliable … In most children, a constant rate of IV fluids based on premorbid weight can be used, and only the duration of IV fluids is adjusted.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Intravenous fluids' (Last updated January 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Intravenous_fluids/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Dehydrated child, maintenance + 5% deficit over 24 hours:** under 4 kg — consult a senior clinician · 5 kg 30 · 10 kg 60 · 20 kg 100 · 30 kg 130 · 40 kg 160 · 50 kg 190 mL/hr.
claims.source_text: Weight (kg) Hourly fluid rate (maintenance + 5% deficit replacement over 24 hours) (mL/hour) <4 kg Consult senior clinician 4 24 5 30 6 36 7 42 8 48 10 60 12 68 14 76 16 84 18 92 20 100 25 115 30 130 35 145 40 160 45 175 50 190

claims.claim: **Deranged electrolytes:** consult a senior clinician and consider slower deficit replacement.
claims.source_text: If electrolytes are deranged, consult senior clinician and relevant guideline, and consider slower replacement of deficit
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Intravenous fluids' (Last updated January 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Intravenous_fluids/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Replace significant ongoing losses** by the previous hour or 4-hour period (e.g. 200 mL over 4 hours → 50 mL/hr for the next 4), commonly with **sodium chloride 0.9% + potassium chloride 20 mmol/L** for GI losses.
claims.source_text: Abnormal ongoing losses should be measured and replaced if clinically indicated, based on each previous hour (if significant) or 4-hour period (eg a 200 mL loss over the previous 4 hours is replaced by giving 50 mL/hr for the next 4 hours) Gastrointestinal tract losses are commonly replaced with sodium chloride 0.9% + potassium chloride 20 mmol/L
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Intravenous fluids' (Last updated January 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Intravenous_fluids/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Use a burette in small children; set pumps to an hourly volume and check it each hour.**
claims.source_text: Using a burette in small children can reduce the risk of large volumes being inadvertently administered IV pumps should be set with an hourly volume to be infused. Reset each hour with the volume infused checked
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Intravenous fluids' (Last updated January 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Intravenous_fluids/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Consider transfer** for severe electrolyte or glucose abnormalities, or **shock needing ≥40 mL/kg of boluses.**
claims.source_text: Consider transfer when Children with severe electrolyte or glucose abnormalities Shock requiring ≥40 mL/kg IV fluid boluses
